newsitem.title: CHINA: China seen stressing market stability - analysts.
newsitem.headline: China seen stressing market stability - analysts.

text.p: The apparent success of China's attempts to cool down its red-hot stock markets could see Chinese authorities now begin to stress market stability, analysts said on Thursday.

Share-price falls since the handover of Hong Kong to China, a slowdown in the pace of new domestic A share issues, and lower returns on new counters have China securities authorities believing the market-dampening measures may no longer be needed, the analysts said.
"The falls since early this month must have been outside the expectations of the securities authorities," said a broker.
"This might lead to a new campaign in the official media, stressing the need to stabilise the markets," he said.
The July 1 return of Hong Kong to Chinese sovereignty after 156 years as a British colony had removed a major positive factor from the markets, the analysts said.
This triggered losses of around 15 percent on the Shenzhen and Shanghai bourses in the first week after the media-hyped handover, and investor confidence took a battering.
"The falls since Hong Kong's return indicate there is no need for the securities authorities to take further measures to cool down stock fever," said an executive with a major Chinese brokerage.
"The pace of new share issues has been greatly slowed down since the start of this month," he said.
Beijing authorities introduced measures in May and June aimed at curbing speculation and cooling the frenzy that lifted indices by about 50 percent in the first half of 1997, the analysts said.
Since the crackdown, official newspapers have carried lengthy warnings against excessive speculation.

But in a sudden change of tone on Wednesday, the Financial Times -- mouthpiece of the central bank, which orchestrated the crackdown -- urged investors not to lose confidence in the stock markets or to blindly sell on market falls.
"The recent cycle of ups and downs on China's stock markets is not compatible with the comparatively stable national economy," the newspaper said in a commentary.
The Shanghai stock exchange has not listed any new shares since the start of July and no new A share issues are scheduled.
The Shenzhen stock exchange is due to list 355 million new shares in four A share companies.
This compares to two billion new shares issued in 37 A share firms on the two exchanges in June, a large number of them issued in the last 10 days of the month.
The markets had been unable to digest the massive influx of new shares, analysts said, and this had contributed to the share price falls.

Returns on new shares had also fallen recently, they said, citing an average rise of 60 percent in a stock's price on its debut, compared with an average 150 percent throughout the first half of the year.
"Some poor-quality firms got the green light for their share issues in the first half with the central government in a hurry to push new shares into the markets," said one stock analyst.
"Now with prices falling, the authorities are expected to tighten new issue control and this will help slow the pace of new issues," he said.
Both A and B shares on the Shanghai and Shenzhen bourses staged technical rallies on Thursday morning as investors went bargain-hunting in the wake of the recent price losses, brokers said.
